# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Old-School Model of Toughness

When college students describe toughness, words like hard-nosed, gritty, playing through pain, stoic, and persevering come to mind. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked highest. The traditional image is a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back into place, or Craig MacTavish, the last NHL player to play without a helmet (retired 1997). This view equates toughness with overcoming obstacles through perseverance, discipline, and stoicism—often pictured as a strong brute of a man.

Bobby Knight exemplifies this model. Over five decades and three universities, he won over 900 games (third all-time), reached five Final Fours, and won three NCAA championships. His 1976 Indiana team went undefeated. Knight defined toughness as “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” His methods included tampons hanging from lockers of players he thought “soft,” frequent cussing, a 1991 tirade (“This is absolute fucking bullshit… I will not put me in that fucking position again”), bringing toilet paper with feces to show players what he thought of them, and choking a player at practice. All in the name of creating toughness founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, and using fear to establish authority.

## Tough Parenting and Authoritarianism

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting styles by two factors: responsiveness (attunement, support, fostering individuality) and demandingness (expectations, control, discipline). Low demandingness + high responsiveness = permissive (too soft). High demandingness + low responsiveness = authoritarian (too hard). Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, punishment; a typical refrain is “You need to do this because I said so.” In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally.” Another study found 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on children. The “just right” Goldilocks fit is high demand accompanied by warmth and understanding. The same principles apply to coaching and leadership: we’ve taken demandingness and forgotten responsiveness.

## Callousness and Machismo

The language of toughness equates it with callousness: “soft,” “hardening up,” “show no signs of weakness.” We romanticize the *Karate Kid* narrative. In youth sports, parents justify making eleven-year-olds go until they puke as necessary “to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior” (Mark Hyman, *Until It Hurts*). Toughness is tied to masculinity: “man up,” “stop being a pussy,” “There’s no crying in baseball!” (from *A League of Their Own*). The image is The Rock or Vin Diesel, not a small female. Yet women consistently handle pain better than men. The old model is callousness and machismo—a myth of an “inner warrior” built on callous demandingness, a remnant of military-style drill sergeants.

## Consequences of the Callous View

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair, 19, showed profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches and trainers yelled to “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” After his final sprint, it took trainers 34 minutes to get him off the field and another 28 minutes to call 911. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke. Rhabdomyolysis (muscle products leaking into bloodstream) has become common from extreme workouts designed to “test” athletes, not improve fitness. As Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, the true notion is to “toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots.”

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport, it’s linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In one study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse with military challenges. The style creates the appearance of discipline without fostering it. One young athlete explained: “Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger… I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished.” The motivation is avoidance of punishment, not internal desire.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance. Real toughness is “experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.”

Pete Carroll, one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl, exemplifies real toughness. He encourages meditation and yoga, shifts from meetings to ring toss if players get heated. According to one star player, “He’s never negative, doesn’t scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive.” Carroll believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, bouncing back. He told *The Bleacher Report*: “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do.” Other successful coaches with similar approaches include Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, and Mike D’Antoni (who told the author, “We keep it positive here”). As Ken Reed summarized, “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach.”

Research from Eastern Washington University (2008) on nearly 200 basketball players concluded: “The ‘keys’ to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach’s ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

## The Author’s Personal Story

The author, a University of Houston runner, collapsed during the Don Bowden Mile (the race named after the first American to break four minutes in 1957). At 900 meters into the 1,609-meter race, he experienced a strange high-pitched gasp and tightening in his neck. His inner focus shattered; he tried all his tricks but couldn’t continue. After a year of tests, allergist Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—the vocal cords shut when they should open, blocking inhalation. The American Thoracic Society cites “strong emotions” and stress as triggers. The author’s old strategy of pushing until he puked backfired. He had to learn to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady at the moment of highest discomfort. This search for what toughness really means became the book.

## The Four Pillars of Real Toughness

1. **Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality**
2. **Listen to Your Body**
3. **Respond Instead of React**
4. **Transcend Discomfort**

## The Basic Categories

Seven primary types of things to track: Projects list, project support material, calendar actions/information, Next Actions lists, Waiting For list, reference material, Someday/Maybe list. These categories must be kept **pristinely distinct**—each represents a discrete type of agreement with yourself. If edges blur, you go psychologically numb to contents. Mixing reference with "to read" items makes you unconscious to the stack; putting day-specific actions on Next Actions lists undermines trust in your calendar; active projects mixed with someday/maybes prevents rigorous action focus.

All you really need are **lists and folders**—sufficient for reminders, reference, and support. Lists can be: (1) a file folder with separate paper notes, (2) an actual list on titled paper in a loose-leaf organizer, or (3) a software list. Don't impose external priority scaffolding that requires constant rearrangement; prioritize intuitively by seeing the whole list against shifting variables.

## Organizing Action Reminders

After processing your in-tray, you'll have 20–70+ pending items. Sort them into meaningful groupings.

**Calendar actions** – Only the "hard landscape": time-specific ("10:00–11:00 meet with Jim") or day-specific ("Call Rachel Tuesday"). Resist putting tasks you'd *like* to do on a specific day but might not; the calendar must be sacred territory reflecting exact commitments, noticeable at a glance while on the run. Example: action on getting a medical checkup was calling to make the appointment—since it took less than two minutes, you did it immediately and put the appointment on the calendar.

**As-Soon-As-Possible actions by context** – The best reminder is by the tool, location, or situation needed. How discrete depends on number of actions and how often contexts change. If you have only 25 next actions, one list might suffice; with 50–100, you need sorting. Leverage energy by grouping similar modes (e.g., crank down Calls list when in phone mode, cruise through computer actions when online).

Common categories:

- **Calls** – Include phone numbers alongside each item; you'd likely make the call if the number is already there vs. having to look it up.
- **At Computer** – Separate "Online" from "At Computer" if you fly without Wi-Fi; on a plane you can't connect, so only list actions that don't require internet. Also consider "Anywhere" for actions doable in any context (e.g., think about an idea, draft a note).
- **Errands** – Track sublists within items (e.g., "hardware store" with sublist of pickups). Location-based reminders (GPS) are a nice option but overoptimistic for total trust—many variables prevent relying solely on them.
- **At Office** – For actions requiring physical presence (purging a cabinet, reviewing a document with staff). "Hotel-ing" (no permanent desk) may require multiple location lists.
- **At Home** – Personal and around-the-house projects (hang print, switch closets). If you work only at home, At Home suffices instead of At Office.
- **Agendas** – Separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorneys, etc., plus standing meetings (staff, board, parent/teacher). Allows collecting items for the next conversation. Add ad hoc as needed (e.g., contractor for a project—create a list for the duration).
- **Read/Review** – Best managed as a physical stack tray or portable folder, not a written list. Reserve only for longer-than-two-minute reading items. Keep edges pristine to stay conscious of inventory. Consider also "Review/Respond" for more rigorous reading requiring deeper focus, and "Review/Watch" for digital media (videos, blogs).

**Waiting For** – Track deliverables from others (e.g., tickets ordered, scanner coming, OK on proposal). Include date requested and agreed due date—"worth its weight in gold" for follow-up ("But I placed the order March twentieth"). Review regularly to check status or light a fire. Keep close to Next Actions lists; responsibility may bounce back and forth. Having the list available when talking to those responsible allows early follow-up ("How's it going with the Gonzalez proposal?") before stress builds.

**Using original item as its own reminder** – Efficient for Read/Review (magazine in tray), bills in "Bills to Pay" folder, receipts in envelope. But dangerous if not reviewed consistently. For e-mail: create @ACTION and @WAITING FOR folders (prefix with @ or - to sort at top). Move actionable e-mails out of "in" to get in-tray to empty. Getting "in" empty means deleted, filed, done (<2 min), or moved to reminder folders. When delegating via e-mail, use "Send and File" if available, or bcc yourself to automatically place a copy in @WAITING FOR. If you rarely have more than one screenful of actionable e-mails, keeping them in inbox may suffice; otherwise use folders. **Caution**: distributing triggers across folders, lists, and e-mail is OK only if you review all categories equally. Digital data offscreen can disappear as a prompt—some revert to paper for physical trust. Avoid mixing different next-action types in one pile (e.g., all service requests together when some need calls, others computer work).

## Organizing Project Reminders

A project is any commitment requiring more than one action step. Create a simple Projects list (digital category, loose-leaf page, or file folder). It's an index of open loops, not a priority-sorted plan. You can't do a project; you can only do action steps. The list's real value is complete review (at least weekly) to ensure action steps defined and nothing slips.

**Value of a complete Projects list**:

- **Critical for control and focus** – Small things (renew driver's license) take as much mental space as big ones (formulate conference agenda) when not tracked.
- **Alleviates subtle tensions** – Projects often morph from simple situations (e.g., daughter's preschool registration problem, invoice dispute). Capturing them creates fresh energy.
- **Core of the Weekly Review** – Marries larger commitments to daily activities; requires the list to be current.
- **Facilitates relationship management** – Enables negotiation of commitments with boss, spouse, staff when allocating limited resources.

**Where to find hidden projects**:

1. **Current activities** – Calendar meetings, action lists, workspaces. Example: conference call about client request → project "Look into possible custom program for Client XYZ"; evening orientation at son's school reveals schedule issue.
2. **Higher-horizon interests** – Professional goals, strategic plans, personal life (kids aging, retirement). Review long-range planning documents.
3. **Current problems, issues, opportunities** – Problems (always a project), process improvements, creative/capacity-building opportunities. Examples: "Look into improving Frederick's relationship with his school," "Resolve situation with landlord," "Get closure on compensation dispute."

**One list or subdivided?** Most find one master inventory best. Common subsorts:

- **Personal/Professional** – But personal needs weekday review; many pressures come from personal aspects slipping.
- **Delegated Projects** – For senior managers; review regularly to ensure progress.
- **Specific Types** – e.g., "Projects—Presentations" for speakers, sales relationships in progress for real estate agents. Some sort by major areas of focus (e.g., parents tracking children, entrepreneur dividing by Finance, Sales, Operations).

**Subprojects** – If big project has independent subpieces (e.g., "Finish new home upgrades" with "Finalize patio," "Upgrade kitchen"), list the big project on Projects list and hold subpieces in support material, or list active independent subprojects separately. If subprojects are dependent (e.g., cannot start kitchen until electrical upgraded), they may have no next actions until preceding steps complete. Example: author's "Move to Amsterdam" was one project for months, then unpacked into fifteen (from "Set up Dutch bank accounts" to "Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara").

**Project support materials** – Resources to support actions, not reminders. Don't use support material as action reminders; that creates mental noise ("Do something about me!"). First add project to Projects list, put actions on appropriate lists, then pull support when doing the action. For Weekly Review, pull the file and check for missing next actions. Avoid using client folders or CRM as action reminders; client info is reference, actions go on action lists. Keep support materials accessible but not as primary reminders.

**Organizing ad hoc project thinking** – Attach notes to list items, use e-mail folders (e.g., "Johnson Partnership—Active" and "Archive"), paper-based files, or loose-leaf notebook pages. Key: consistently look for action steps in notes and review as needed. Clear out stale notes to avoid the "stale virus" of redundant information. Avoid spreading data across too many locations without coordinating links.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

Nonactionable items: reference materials, someday/maybes, trash.

**Reference materials** – Once distinguished from actionable, they're just your library. No psychological weight. General-reference filing (1–4 physical drawers, dozens of e-mail folders). Large-category filing (if >50 folders, give own section). Contact managers – purely reference; don't use for action reminders. Libraries/archives – decide what you need with you always, in office, or archived. No perfect system; start from ground up. Example: author's foodie database has hundreds of folders for restaurants worldwide. The Web itself is a huge digital filing cabinet; distinguish nonactionable from actionable inputs.

**Someday/Maybe list** – For things you might want to do later (e.g., "Learn Spanish," "Get Marcie a horse," "Climb Mt. Washington," "Write a mystery novel," "Get a vacation cottage"). Populate from creative imaginings (hobbies, skills, trips) and reassess current projects – move optional projects here if no time for months. Subcategorize if helpful (home projects vs. bucket list). Avoid "Hold and Review" piles – they numb you; in virtually every case, the person held but didn't review, and after processing often nothing remains. The value of someday/maybe disappears without consistent conscious review. You may be surprised that some items happen almost without effort – e.g., learning to play the flute or sail started there for the author.

**Using calendar for future options** – Three creative uses:

- **Triggers for activating projects** – Place a reminder on a future date to add the project to Projects list (e.g., "Add annual sales conference" three months ahead).
- **Events you might participate in** – Put trigger when decision time nears (e.g., seminar registration deadline).
- **Decision catalysts** – Set a future reminder for major decisions you're deferring (hire/fire, change career, strategy redirection). "It's OK to decide not to decide – as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system."

**Tickler file** – 43 folders (31 daily, 12 monthly). Perpetual file: each day empty that day's folder into in-tray, refile at back (daily becomes same day next month; monthly becomes same month next year). Allows storing actual documents (forms, agendas, invoices to pay later). Must check daily to trust system; if you leave town, check folders for days you'll be away before you go.

## Checklists

Checklists are "recipes of potential ingredients" for projects, processes, events, areas of responsibility. They extend the number of operations you can perform without thinking (Whitehead). For fuzzy commitments like "Exercise more regularly," first identify inherent projects and actions ("Set up regular exercise program" / "Call Sally for gym suggestions"). For ongoing areas (e.g., "Maintain good morale on my team"), create overview checklists reviewed regularly. The more novel the situation, the more control needed – e.g., stepping into a new role, learning a new software fix; use checklists until procedures become automatic. Be open to ad hoc checklists ("Things to Take Camping," "Year-end Activities," "Travel Checklist," "Key Clients," "People to Stay in Touch With," "Personal Development"). Capability to instantly make and use checklists is core to high-performance self-management. Keep an easily accessed place (notebook or software) to create and eliminate them as needed.

For ongoing areas (e.g., "Maintain good morale on my team"), create overview checklists reviewed regularly. The more novel the situation, the more control needed. Be open to ad hoc checklists (e.g., "Things to Take Camping," "Year-end Activities"). Capability to instantly make and use checklists is core to high-performance self-management.
